extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write mathematical proofs (introductory proofs course)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and concrete strategies for constructing and writing mathematical proofs (conditionals, negations, contrapositives, contradiction, quantifiers), including scratch-work techniques and how to present the final write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove a conclusion of the form P → Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume P is true and then prove Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating P as assumed is the same as adding P to your list of hypotheses (givens) and changing the goal from P → Q to Q. Scratch-work should show the transformation (givens and goal before and after); the final proof typically begins 'Suppose P.' followed by the proof of Q and ends 'Therefore P → Q.' Note this strategy supplies the first and last sentences but usually leaves a gap of steps in the middle to be filled in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove by contrapositive for conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Because P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P, you can prove P → Q by proving its contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same strategy for conditionals: assume ¬Q and prove ¬P. The final proof begins 'Suppose Q is false.' [Proof of ¬P] 'Therefore P → Q.' Choose this method if it seems to make the problem easier (try both if unsure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Track givens and goals (scratch work vs final proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep track of the statements known or assumed at a point (givens) and the statement that remains to be proven (goal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transforming a problem, update the givens and goal lists. Scratch work may show many transformations; the final write-up usually omits scratch-work and only contains the justifications required to derive the conclusion from the givens (with occasional brief explanation of strategy if proof is complicated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reasoning (scratch work) from final write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasoning used to discover a proof (scratch work) is different from the steps written in the final proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final proofs usually omit how the mathematician thought of the transformations and focus on logical justifications. Include only the sentences needed to justify steps; if helpful in very complicated proofs, a brief explanation of strategy may be provided to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of final proof for P → Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Final proof should start with 'Suppose P.' then include the proof of Q and conclude 'Therefore P → Q.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suggested form tells how the beginning and end of the proof will go, but you must fill in the middle with inferences justified from givens or previously proved statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove a goal of the form ¬P: reexpress when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, reexpress the negated goal as an equivalent positive statement and then use a proof strategy for that form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logical equivalences (DeMorgan's law, conditional laws, definitions) to rewrite ¬P into a more tractable positive goal. Example: 'a ∉ A\B' rewritten to 'a ∈ A → a ∈ B'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume P is true and try to reach a contradiction, thereby concluding ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform the problem by adding P to the givens and set the goal to 'contradiction'. Final proof: 'Suppose P.' [derive contradiction] 'Thus P is false.' Advantage: gives extra assumption to work with; disadvantage: goal is vague (produce any contradiction). Often used when positive reexpression isn't available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a given of the form ¬P in contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a given ¬P and are doing a proof by contradiction, try making P your goal; proving P produces a direct contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using: givens include ¬P and you aim for contradiction. After using: set goal to P and show P follows from other givens. The contradiction with the given ¬P finishes the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexpress givens of the form ¬P
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, rewrite a given ¬P into an equivalent positive form using definitions or logical equivalences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes rewriting a negative given helps apply other strategies. Example: rewriting 'a ∉ B\C' into 'a ∈ B → a ∈ C' makes modus ponens applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use givens of the form P → Q (rules of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are given P → Q, and you have P (or can prove P), then you may conclude Q (modus ponens). If you have ¬Q (or can prove ¬Q), then you may conclude ¬P (modus tollens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label these rules explicitly in scratch-work and, when their antecedents become available, apply them immediately and add the inferred conclusion to the givens list. Names: modus ponens and modus tollens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backwards using rules of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: If your goal is Q and you have a given P → Q, try setting P as a subgoal; proving P allows applying modus ponens to obtain Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This backward reasoning can simplify problem by reducing it to proving P instead of Q. Add the intermediate goal to the scratch-work and proceed until it becomes obvious or follows from givens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions to discover logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out definitions of mathematical terms or set-notation to reveal logical connectives and structure useful for proof strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly expand phrases like 'x ∈ A\C' into 'x ∈ A and x ∉ C' to expose negations/implications that suggest particular strategies (e.g., contradiction, modus ponens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Try several strategies; choose based on logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple strategies apply (assume antecedent, contrapositive, contradiction, etc.), you may need to try several before finding one that works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With practice, you will get better at guessing which strategy is most likely to work for a particular proof. Transform the problem repeatedly (updating givens and goal) until the remaining problem is straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ordinary English in final proofs; avoid logical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Although logical symbols are helpful in scratch work, mathematicians usually try to avoid them in final write-ups and use ordinary English instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using formal logic in scratch work is beneficial for strategy-finding, but the final proof should read naturally in English while still providing complete justifications of steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: You do not need to identify which assumption fails after a contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contradiction is reached from the givens plus an extra assumption, you need only conclude that the extra assumption (the one you introduced) must be false relative to the original givens; you do not have to determine which of the three statements in the combined list is the culprit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a proof of an implication via contradiction, if adding the assumed antecedent together with original givens leads to contradiction, infer that the antecedent cannot hold when the givens hold, completing the proof. The scratch-work demonstration clarifies this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format inner proofs and nesting in complex conditionals/contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements like ¬R → (P → ¬Q), nest assumptions and present the inner proof indented or conceptually separated: assume ¬R, assume P, deduce Q → R by modus ponens, then use ¬R to get ¬Q by modus tollens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the givens/goal scratch-work to keep track of nested assumptions, and then convert that structure into a linear final proof: 'Suppose ¬R. Suppose P. Since P and P → (Q → R), ...' finishing with the derived conditional statements.
